beginner: Plant watermelon in light, well-drained soil that warms up fast, like a sandy loam, with some compost mixed in. Avoid going overboard on rich, high-nitrogen material, because that gives you lots of leaves and vine but less fruit. Many gardeners plant on low hills or raised mounds, which warm up and drain better and keep the fruit off soggy ground. If your soil is heavy clay, it stays cold and wet and can bring on disease, so mix in compost and build the soil up into mounds, or pick the sandiest, best-draining spot you have.
seasoned: Watermelon does best in deep, well-drained, light soil, with sandy loams and loamy sands the classic choice because they warm quickly in spring and drain freely, which this heat-loving, deep-rooted crop rewards. Work a few inches of compost into the bed before planting, but go easier on nitrogen-rich amendments than you would for leafy crops, since too much nitrogen pushes vine at the expense of fruit and sugar. Many growers plant on low, wide hills or raised mounds, which warm faster, drain better, and lift the crown and developing fruit off wet ground. Heavy clay holds water and stays cold, slowing growth and inviting Fusarium wilt and fruit rot, so amend it generously and build mounds, or grow on sandier ground.

beginner: Watermelon likes soil that is slightly acidic to neutral, about pH 6.0 to 6.8, and most garden soil is already close. An inexpensive soil test tells you where you stand and whether you need to adjust it before planting.
seasoned: Watermelon grows best in slightly acidic to neutral soil, around pH 6.0 to 6.8, and tolerates a wider band of roughly 5.5 to 7.5. It is a little more forgiving of mildly acidic ground than many vegetables, but strongly acidic or strongly alkaline soil tightens nutrient uptake. Test before planting and lime or add sulfur only on the test's advice rather than by guess.

beginner: Watermelon does not need a lot of nitrogen, and too much gives you big leafy vines but fewer, less sweet melons. Mix a fertilizer that is lower in nitrogen, like a 5-10-10, into the soil before planting, then give the plants a little nitrogen when the vines start to run and again when flowers appear. Once the melons start to form, stop pushing nitrogen so the plant puts its energy into growing sweet fruit instead of more leaves.
seasoned: Watermelon is a moderate feeder that wants more phosphorus and potassium than nitrogen, since excess nitrogen drives leafy vine at the expense of fruit set and sugar. Work a lower-nitrogen complete fertilizer such as 5-10-10 into the bed before planting (Clemson suggests about 30 pounds per 1,000 square feet), then side-dress with a nitrogen source as the vines begin to run, and again lightly at flowering. Ease off nitrogen once fruit has set so the plant pours its energy into sizing and sweetening the melons rather than growing more vine. Pair feeding with even moisture, because the nutrients only help a plant that is not also drought-stressed.

beginner: Your watermelon vines are spreading. Give them a light feeding of nitrogen now.
seasoned: Your watermelon vines are running, time to side-dress with a little nitrogen. Then keep feeding light and ease off nitrogen once fruit sets, so the plant builds sweet melons rather than vine.

beginner: Use a lower-nitrogen fertilizer like 5-10-10 at planting, then a little nitrogen as the vines spread. Do not overdo the nitrogen once melons form, or you get leaves instead of fruit.
seasoned: A lower-nitrogen complete fertilizer such as 5-10-10 worked in at planting, then a nitrogen side-dress as the vines run and again lightly at flowering, easing off nitrogen once fruit sets. Too much nitrogen gives vine and leaf at the expense of fruit and sweetness.

beginner: Mix a lower-nitrogen fertilizer or a few inches of compost into the soil before planting. Then feed with a little nitrogen about three to four weeks later, scratched into the soil a few inches away from the plants, and once more when flowers appear.
seasoned: A common approach is a lower-nitrogen complete fertilizer such as 5-10-10 worked into the bed before planting (Clemson cites about 30 pounds per 1,000 square feet, or a balanced scoop per hill), then a nitrogen side-dress about three to four weeks after planting as vines run, placed a few inches out from the plants and watered in, repeated lightly at flowering.

beginner: The most useful watermelon companions are flowers that bring in bees, since watermelon needs lots of bee visits to set fruit (especially seedless kinds, which depend on bees carrying pollen from a seeded variety). Bush beans add a little nitrogen, and nasturtiums can lure pests away. The one rule that really matters is to keep watermelon away from other melons, cucumbers, and squash, which all share the same pests and diseases.
seasoned: Most watermelon companion pairings are traditional rather than trial-tested, and the ones worth acting on serve two practical ends: pollination and pest pressure. Because watermelon fruit set is strongly pollinator-limited, flowering insectary plants like borage near the patch are a genuine help, and that help is doubly important if you grow seedless types, which lean entirely on bees moving pollen from a seeded pollinizer. Bush beans fix nitrogen the crop can use without the heavy feeding that would otherwise grow vine over fruit, and a trap planting of nasturtium can divert cucumber beetles and other pests. The firmest rule is a rotation one: keep watermelon away from other cucurbits, which share its pest and disease complex, including the soilborne Fusarium wilt and the foliar anthracnose and gummy stem blight that build up where melons follow melons.

beginner: Borage flowers are loved by bees, and watermelon needs lots of bee visits to set fruit, so a few borage plants nearby can help with pollination. This matters most for seedless watermelon, which depends on bees.
seasoned: A strong bee magnet whose flowers recruit the pollinators watermelon fruit set depends on, which is especially valuable for seedless types that rely on bees moving pollen from a seeded pollinizer. Pollinator-habitat value is well grounded; the specific borage-watermelon pairing is traditional rather than trial-tested.

beginner: Beans pull nitrogen from the air into the soil, which watermelon can use, and they do not share watermelon's pests. A good, traditional neighbor.
seasoned: Bush beans fix nitrogen that lightly benefits the crop without the heavy nitrogen that would push vine over fruit, and they share none of the cucurbit pests. A traditional, mechanistically plausible pairing rather than a trial-isolated one.

beginner: Nasturtiums are often grown near melons and squash to lure cucumber beetles and other pests away, and their flowers bring in bees. A helpful, low-risk neighbor.
seasoned: Often planted near cucurbits as a trap and deterrent for cucumber beetles, and its flowers also draw the bees watermelon depends on for fruit set. Trap cropping is a documented principle, but the specific nasturtium-watermelon effect is not formally isolated, so treat it as a plausible aid.

beginner: Corn is the traditional Three Sisters partner that gives sprawling vines something to grow among. With watermelon it is more tradition than a proven boost, and watermelon's full-sun need means you should not let corn shade it much.
seasoned: The classic Three Sisters partner, though the fit is looser for watermelon than for shade-tolerant squash: tall corn can give the trailing vines structure, but watermelon wants full sun to sweeten, so keep corn from shading the patch. A long-standing intercropping tradition with a space rationale, not a measured yield effect for this pair.

beginner: Keep watermelon away from other melons, cucumbers, and squash. They share most of the same pests and diseases, so planting them together makes those problems worse.
seasoned: Cucumber, muskmelon, squash, and pumpkin share watermelon's pest and disease complex, including cucumber beetle, aphid-spread mosaic viruses, the mildews, and the soilborne Fusarium wilt and foliar anthracnose and gummy stem blight that build up where cucurbits repeat. Grouping them concentrates that pressure. A real epidemiology and rotation principle rather than a tested adjacency effect: spread cucurbits out and rotate them on a long cycle.

beginner: Some gardeners keep potatoes and melons apart, since both are hungry plants and potatoes can bring their own diseases. This is more tradition than a proven rule.
seasoned: A traditional caution that potatoes and cucurbits compete heavily and that potatoes can harbor disease and attract pests near melons. There is no strong T1 mechanism for the specific pairing, so it persists mostly as garden lore.

beginner: Small yellow beetles with stripes or spots chew on the leaves and flowers of young plants and can scar the fruit. They can also spread disease, though watermelon handles the wilt disease better than cucumbers or cantaloupe.
seasoned: Small striped or spotted yellow beetles chew young leaves, stems, flowers, and the rind of developing fruit, and can enter the soil to feed on seedlings below ground. The bigger threat is indirect: cucumber beetles can transmit bacterial wilt and spread mosaic viruses, though watermelon is far less prone to bacterial wilt collapse than cucumber and muskmelon.

beginner: Cucumber beetles spend the winter as adults and move onto young plants early. They feed on the leaves and can carry diseases from plant to plant, and seedlings are most at risk.
seasoned: Striped and spotted cucumber beetles feed on cucurbits and overwinter as adults, colonizing plants early in the season. They carry the bacterial wilt organism in their gut and spread mosaic viruses as they feed; seedlings are most vulnerable.

beginner: Cover young plants with a light row cover (take it off when flowers open so bees can reach them), pick beetles off by hand, and clear away weeds. Yellow sticky traps help, and strong young plants shrug off some feeding.
seasoned: Protect seedlings with floating row cover removed at flowering for pollination, hand-pick beetles, and clear weeds that shelter them. Yellow sticky traps help monitor and reduce numbers; keep young plants vigorous so they grow past the most vulnerable stage.

beginner: Cover seedlings until they flower, keep them growing strong, clear away weeds and old plants, and do not plant where melons or squash grew last year.
seasoned: Exclude beetles from seedlings with row cover, keep plants growing fast, clear weeds and debris, and rotate away from where cucurbits grew. Aim control at the early-season colonizers.

beginner: Tiny soft insects gather under the leaves and on new growth, making leaves curl and yellow, often with a sticky film. They can also spread viruses that damage the plant.
seasoned: Colonies of small soft-bodied insects, often melon aphids, cluster on leaf undersides and growing tips, curling and yellowing the leaves and coating them in sticky honeydew that grows sooty mold. Beyond direct feeding, melon aphids transmit mosaic viruses that mottle and distort the foliage and can ruin a crop.

beginner: Aphids are small insects that suck the plant's juices and multiply quickly, especially on soft, over-fed growth. The sticky honeydew they leave grows black mold, and they can carry plant viruses.
seasoned: Melon and other aphids suck sap and multiply rapidly in warm weather, building up fast on stressed or over-fertilized plants, and typically colonize once the vines begin to run. The honeydew they excrete fosters sooty mold, and several species spread cucurbit mosaic viruses.

beginner: Blast them off with a strong spray of water and treat the undersides of the leaves with insecticidal soap, repeating every few days. Ladybugs and other helpful insects eat aphids, so welcome them.
seasoned: Knock colonies off with a strong jet of water and spray insecticidal soap or horticultural oil with thorough coverage of leaf undersides, repeating every few days. Conserve ladybugs, lacewings, and parasitic wasps, which usually bring aphids under control; reflective mulch deters them from young plants.

beginner: Do not over-fertilize with nitrogen, check the undersides of leaves regularly, and let helpful insects do their work. A reflective mulch around young plants helps keep aphids away.
seasoned: Avoid excess nitrogen, which drives the soft growth aphids favor, scout leaf undersides and growing tips, and support natural enemies rather than spraying broadly. Reflective or aluminum-foil mulch deters aphids from young plants.

beginner: The leaves get a fine yellow or bronze speckling, and in bad cases you see tiny webs underneath. Spider mites love hot, dry weather and can build up fast on watermelon in summer.
seasoned: Pale yellow and reddish-brown stippling appears on the upper sides of leaves, ranging from small specks to large whitish, stippled areas, and fine webbing shows on leaf undersides in bad infestations. Two-spotted spider mites explode in hot, dry weather, exactly watermelon's season, and heavy feeding bronzes and dries the foliage, cutting fruit size and sugar.

beginner: Tiny mites that thrive in hot, dry summers and multiply fast, especially after broad insecticide sprays kill the helpful bugs that normally keep them down. They feed on the undersides of the leaves.
seasoned: Two-spotted spider mites are tiny sap-feeders that proliferate during hot, dry weather and whose populations explode rapidly when their natural enemies are killed off by broad-spectrum sprays. They feed mostly on leaf undersides.

beginner: Spray the plants, especially the undersides of the leaves, with a strong stream of water, and treat with insecticidal soap or horticultural oil if needed. Avoid spraying broad insecticides, which kill the good bugs that eat mites.
seasoned: Spray plants with a strong jet of water to dislodge mites and raise humidity, and apply insecticidal soap or horticultural oil with thorough leaf-underside coverage before populations peak, repeating as needed. Avoid broad-spectrum insecticides, which kill the predatory mites and insects that control them.

beginner: Keep plants watered so they are not stressed in the heat, and avoid spraying strong insecticides that kill helpful bugs. Check under the leaves during hot, dry weather and treat early if you see speckling.
seasoned: Keep plants well watered and not heat-stressed, since drought-stressed plants are hit hardest, and avoid broad-spectrum insecticides that wipe out natural enemies. Scout leaf undersides through hot, dry spells and act early.

beginner: Leaves get yellow spots, then brown and wilt, and you find clusters of shield-shaped gray-brown bugs and their bronze eggs under the leaves. Watermelon is not their favorite, but they can still bother young plants.
seasoned: Leaves develop yellow specks that brown and wilt, and heavily fed runners can wilt and turn brittle. Flat bronze egg clusters appear on leaf undersides along the veins, and gray-brown adults and pale nymphs cluster near the crown and under debris. Watermelon is less affected than winter squash, but young plants can still be hurt.

beginner: Squash bugs pierce the leaves and stems and suck out the juices, which makes the vines wilt. They hide in plant debris over winter and prefer squash to watermelon, but can still attack young plants.
seasoned: The squash bug feeds with piercing-sucking mouthparts on cucurbit foliage and stems, injecting saliva that wilts and browns the tissue. There is one generation a year in much of the South, and adults overwinter in garden debris. It prefers squash and pumpkin to watermelon.

beginner: Pick the bugs off by hand and scrape off the egg clusters under the leaves. A board laid on the ground overnight draws them underneath, then lift it in the morning and destroy them. Treat the young bugs with insecticidal soap.
seasoned: Hand-pick adults, crush the bronze egg masses on leaf undersides, and trap bugs by laying a board near the plants overnight, then lifting it in the morning and destroying the cluster underneath. Target young nymphs with insecticidal soap, since adults are tough to kill.

beginner: Clean up old vines after harvest so the bugs have nowhere to overwinter, move your melons around the garden each year, and check under the leaves for eggs early in the season.
seasoned: Clean up vines and debris at season's end to cut overwintering sites, rotate cucurbits, and scout leaf undersides for the bronze egg clusters from early in the season, acting before nymphs mature.

beginner: On many squash, a healthy plant suddenly wilts in summer with sawdust-like specks at a hole near the base of the stem, and a fat white grub inside. Watermelon rarely gets this, since the borer mostly leaves it alone, but it is still worth a look.
seasoned: On susceptible squash a vine wilts suddenly in midsummer with sawdust-like frass oozing from a hole low on the stem and a fat white caterpillar inside. Watermelon is the fortunate exception: the borer rarely attacks watermelon or cucumber, so this collapse is uncommon, though heavy local pressure can occasionally produce damage.

beginner: A moth lays eggs at the base of squash stems in early summer and the grubs tunnel inside, but the moth strongly prefers thin-stemmed squash like zucchini and mostly leaves watermelon alone.
seasoned: The larva of the squash vine borer moth bores into thin-stemmed Cucurbita pepo squash; it largely avoids watermelon and cucumber, so watermelon planted near a borer-ravaged zucchini usually sails through untouched. Where pressure is severe, an occasional larva may still enter.

beginner: Watermelon seldom needs treatment. If you do find a borer, slit the stem with a knife, dig out the grub, and cover the spot with damp soil so it can re-root.
seasoned: Rarely needed on watermelon. If a borer does enter, slit the stem lengthwise, remove the larva, and bury that node under moist soil to re-root; remove badly damaged vines.

beginner: Growing watermelon is half the battle, since the borer mostly skips it. If borers are bad where you live, cover young plants with a light row cover until they flower, then take it off so bees can pollinate.
seasoned: Choosing watermelon is itself most of the prevention, since the borer mostly avoids it. Where pressure is severe, row cover from planting until flowering excludes the egg-laying moths, and tilling in late winter and rotating disrupts overwintering pupae.

beginner: Dark brown-black spots show up on the older leaves and grow into ragged patches, and the fruit can get sunken dark spots on the rind. In wet weather the spots may look pink-orange. Bad cases strip the leaves off the vine.
seasoned: Small brown-black spots appear first on the older crown leaves, expanding into ragged, sometimes water-soaked lesions; in damp weather the spots carry orange-pink spore masses that turn gray as it dries. On fruit it causes sunken, dark spots on the rind that can keep developing in transit and storage, and severe infection defoliates the vines.

beginner: A fungus that thrives in warm, wet weather and spreads from infected seed and old plant debris. It is worse on late plantings and in rainy spells.
seasoned: Anthracnose is caused by the seed-borne fungus Colletotrichum, favored by warm, damp weather and prolonged leaf wetness, and it hits late plantings especially hard. It overwinters on infected debris and seed.

beginner: Treat early, at the first spots, with a labeled fungicide and remove badly affected leaves and fruit. Water the soil, not the leaves, and stay out of the patch when the vines are wet.
seasoned: Treat at the first spots with a labeled fungicide such as chlorothalonil or mancozeb, covering both leaf surfaces, and remove the worst-affected leaves and fruit. Avoid overhead watering and working among wet vines. Once it is widespread, control is mostly damage limitation.

beginner: Choose resistant varieties and clean seed, rotate where you grow melons so they are not in the same spot every year, water at the base, and remove sick leaves and fruit early.
seasoned: Plant resistant varieties and disease-free seed, do not soak seed before planting, rotate watermelon and other cucurbits out of the bed for several years, water at the base, and start a protective spray schedule before the disease appears in wet seasons.

beginner: You see round black spots on the leaves and dark sunken patches on the stems, sometimes with a brown gummy ooze. The leaf spots grow fast into big tan blotches, and in warm, wet weather the vines can collapse.
seasoned: Round, black, wrinkled spots form on young leaves and dark, sunken, sometimes girdling lesions develop on the stems, often with a brown gummy ooze on the surface. Brownish circular leaf spots expand rapidly into large tan lesions, and a brown streak can appear at the blossom end of the fruit. In warm, wet weather the foliage and vines can collapse quickly.

beginner: A fungus that spreads in warm, wet weather, especially in the South, and survives on seed and old plant debris. Long rainy spells make it move fast.
seasoned: Gummy stem blight is caused by the seed-borne fungus Didymella bryoniae (Stagonosporopsis), a warm-weather, southern cucurbit disease driven by prolonged rainy periods and leaf wetness. It survives on seed and infected debris.

beginner: Use a labeled fungicide at the first sign and remove the worst vines. Give plants room so air moves between them, and water at the base to keep the leaves dry.
seasoned: Start a protective fungicide schedule at the first sign, covering leaf undersides, and remove and destroy badly affected vines. Improve airflow, avoid overhead irrigation, and keep the foliage as dry as possible.

beginner: Pick resistant varieties and clean seed, rotate where you grow melons, give plants room, water at the base, and keep an eye out in warm, humid weather.
seasoned: Plant resistant varieties and clean seed, rotate cucurbits out of the bed for several years, space plants for airflow, water at the soil line, and avoid working among wet vines. Scout closely in warm, humid weather.

beginner: The leaves turn yellow and wilt, often on just one runner at first, and the plant dies even though the soil is wet. You may see a pinkish mold near the base of a dying stem. It is the most serious soil disease of watermelon.
seasoned: Foliage turns yellow and wilts, often starting on one side or one runner, and infected plants decline and die soon after symptoms appear even though the soil is moist. A pinkish-white cottony growth can show near the soil line on dying stems, and a cut stem reveals browned, discolored vascular tissue. It is the most damaging soilborne disease of watermelon.

beginner: A soil fungus that only attacks watermelon, blocking the plant's water pipes so it wilts. It builds up in warm, sandy soil and survives for years, which is why long rotations matter.
seasoned: Fusarium wilt is caused by the soilborne fungus Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. niveum, which is specific to watermelon and clogs the water-conducting tissue. It thrives in warm, sandy soils typical of watermelon ground and persists in soil for many years; several races exist, and resistance covers only some of them.

beginner: There is no cure once a plant has it, so pull and destroy infected plants. You cannot spray it away, so prevention is everything.
seasoned: There is no cure once a plant is infected; remove and destroy wilting plants. Management is preventive and cultural, since fungicides do not control a soilborne vascular wilt.

beginner: Choose resistant varieties, do not grow watermelon in the same ground for at least five years, and where the disease is bad, look into grafted plants on resistant roots. Keep plants healthy and do not overwater.
seasoned: Plant resistant varieties, follow a long rotation of at least five years out of watermelon and related cucurbits, and consider grafting onto resistant rootstock where the disease is established. Avoid moving infested soil, and keep plants vigorous but not over-watered.

beginner: A white, powdery coating spreads over the leaves until they yellow, brown, and die. The plant fades early, and the melons may not size up or sweeten well.
seasoned: White, powdery patches appear on the upper and lower leaf surfaces and stems, spreading until leaves yellow, brown, and die back ahead of schedule. Early defoliation cuts the season short, reduces fruit size and sugar, and exposes melons to sunscald.

beginner: A fungus that spreads on warm, humid days, especially where plants are crowded and air does not move well. It does not need wet leaves to take hold.
seasoned: Powdery mildew fungi thrive in warm conditions with high humidity but do not need leaf wetness, spreading by wind-blown spores. Crowded plantings, poor airflow, and shade worsen it, and it is a common late-season cucurbit disease.

beginner: Treat early, at the first white spots, with a labeled fungicide like sulfur or horticultural oil, and remove badly affected leaves. Water the soil, not the leaves.
seasoned: Treat at the first spots with a labeled fungicide such as sulfur or a horticultural oil or biofungicide, covering both leaf surfaces, and remove the worst leaves. Avoid overhead watering. Once it is widespread, control is mostly damage limitation.

beginner: Pick resistant varieties, give plants plenty of room and full sun, water at the base, and start checking in midsummer, treating the first white spots early.
seasoned: Choose resistant varieties, space plants for airflow, plant in full sun, and avoid excess nitrogen and overhead watering. Scout from midsummer and treat at the first sign.

beginner: Yellow, angular patches show on top of the leaves with fuzzy gray-purple growth underneath, mostly in damp, humid weather. The spots brown and spread, and badly hit leaves can die within a couple of weeks.
seasoned: Small yellowish, angular areas bounded by the leaf veins appear on the upper leaf surface, water-soaked underneath with a grayish or purplish fuzzy spore growth in humid weather. Lesions turn from yellow to brown and several infected leaves can die within 10 to 14 days, rapidly defoliating the vines.

beginner: A mold-like disease that blows in on the wind during mild, rainy weather and needs wet leaves to infect. It can move through a planting quickly.
seasoned: Downy mildew is caused by the air-borne, fungus-like water mold Pseudoperonospora cubensis, which needs leaf wetness and humidity to infect and arrives on wind currents during mild, rainy stretches, often spreading north through the season from overwintering sites in the far South.

beginner: Open up the planting so leaves dry faster, remove the worst leaves, and use a labeled fungicide when wet weather sets in. Do not water over the leaves.
seasoned: Improve airflow, let foliage dry, remove badly affected leaves, and apply a labeled fungicide covering leaf undersides when conditions favor the disease. Avoid overhead irrigation, which keeps leaves wet.

beginner: Give plants room so air moves between them, water at the base, choose resistant varieties if downy mildew is common where you live, and watch closely in humid weather.
seasoned: Space for airflow, water at the soil line rather than overhead, choose resistant varieties where available, and start protective sprays when the disease is reported moving into your area. Scout closely in humid weather.

beginner: Give watermelon about 1 to 2 inches of water a week, more when it is hot and dry. Water deeply rather than a little every day, since the plant roots deep and the fruit is almost all water.
seasoned: Aim for about 1 to 2 inches of water per week, more in heat or on sandy soil, delivered deeply and less often rather than in light daily sprinkles. Watermelon is deep-rooted, with the bulk of its roots in the top 12 inches, and the fruit is about 92 percent water, so steady moisture through fruit sizing is essential.

beginner: About 1 to 2 inches of water a week is a good target, more while the plant is flowering and the melons are growing.
seasoned: Around 1 to 2 inches per week is the working range, leaning higher during flowering and fruit sizing and through hot, dry spells. Even, deep watering builds large, well-filled melons; let the plant swing dry and you get poor set, small fruit, and blossom-end and hollow-heart problems.

beginner: Water the soil, not the leaves, using a soaker hose or watering wand at the base, which helps prevent leaf disease. As the melons get close to ripe, ease off the water. That last step is what makes watermelon sweet, since too much water near harvest waters down the flavor and can crack the fruit.
seasoned: Water at the base with drip or a soaker hose, keeping the foliage as dry as possible, since wet leaves invite anthracnose, gummy stem blight, and the mildews that watermelon is prone to. The key move unique to watermelon is to taper watering as the fruit approaches ripeness, which concentrates the sugars and sweetens the flesh, while over-watering near harvest dilutes flavor and can split fruit.

beginner: If lower leaves yellow, the plant wilts even though the soil is wet, stems go soft, or the melons split or taste watery, it is getting too much water or the soil drains poorly.
seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves, wilting even when the soil is wet, soft or rotting stems, and split or bland, watery fruit point to overwatering or poor drainage. Saturated soil also favors Fusarium wilt and fruit rot, especially on heavy ground.

beginner: Some midday wilting in hot weather is normal and passes by evening. Leaves that stay wilted mean the plant is too dry, and drought while fruit is forming gives small, misshapen melons.
seasoned: Midday wilting that recovers overnight is normal in heat, but leaves that stay limp and dull signal real drought. Dry spells during fruit sizing show up as small, misshapen melons, aborted young fruit, and blossom-end problems.

beginner: Keep the soil evenly damp until the seedlings come up. Watermelon is sown into warm ground, so do not let the surface dry out over the seeds.
seasoned: Direct-sown into warm soil, watermelon wants the seedbed kept evenly moist until emergence; do not let the surface crust over the germinating seed.

beginner: Keep the young plants evenly watered as they get going.
seasoned: Grow the young plants on with steady, even moisture as they start to run.

beginner: Water deeply at the base, about 1 to 2 inches a week and more when hot. Watermelon roots deep, so a good soak beats a light daily sprinkle. Keep the leaves dry to avoid disease.
seasoned: Watermelon is deep-rooted, with most roots in the top 12 inches, so water deeply at the base, about 1 to 2 inches a week and more in heat, with drip or a soaker hose to keep the disease-prone foliage dry against anthracnose, gummy stem blight, and mildews.

beginner: Keep the water even once flowers open, so the melons set well.
seasoned: Flowering through fruit set opens the water-critical stretch. Steady moisture drives good set; a dry check gives poor set and aborted young fruit.

beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist while the melons size up. The fruit is almost all water, so a dry spell now gives small melons with hollow centers.
seasoned: Fruit sizing is the peak: the fruit is about 92 percent water, so steady, deep moisture builds large, well-filled melons, while a dry-to-wet swing gives small fruit, hollow heart, and blossom-end problems.

beginner: Here is the trick that makes watermelon sweet: ease off the water in the last week or two before you pick. Too much water right before harvest waters down the flavor and can crack the melon.
seasoned: The move unique to melons: deliberately taper watering in the last week or two before harvest to concentrate the sugars and sweeten the flesh. Over-watering near ripeness dilutes flavor and can split the fruit.

beginner: Watering the soil instead of the leaves is the best thing you can do for watermelon. It keeps the plant healthy without encouraging leaf disease, and easing off near harvest makes the fruit sweeter.
seasoned: Base watering is the most useful habit for watermelon, because the same plant that wants steady moisture through sizing is also disease-prone when its leaves stay wet. Keep water on the soil and air moving through the leaves, then ease off as the fruit nears ripeness to concentrate the sugars.

beginner: The most important time to keep watermelon watered is when it is flowering and the fruit is growing. Then ease off in the last week or two before harvest so the melon turns sweet.
seasoned: The water-critical stretch is flowering through fruit set and sizing. Steady moisture here drives large, well-filled melons; uneven water gives poor set, small fruit, and hollow heart. Then deliberately taper watering in the last week or two before harvest to sweeten the flesh.

beginner: You pick a watermelon once, when it is fully ripe, and it will not get any riper after you cut it, so timing matters. Look for several signs together: the little curly tendril closest to the melon dries up and turns brown; the pale spot where the melon sits on the ground turns creamy yellow instead of white; the skin goes from shiny to dull; and the melon makes a deep, dull thump when you tap it, instead of a tight, high ring. beginner: You plant watermelon once for the season. It grows through the summer and ripens its melons in mid to late summer, so there is no need to replant every few weeks. seasoned: Watermelon is not a succession crop. beginner: Each regular watermelon plant has both male and female flowers, so one plant can make fruit by itself. Bees carry the pollen between the flowers, and watermelon needs a lot of bee visits to set each melon, so anything that brings bees to your garden helps. The one big exception is seedless watermelon: those plants cannot pollinate themselves, so you have to plant a regular seeded variety nearby (often one seeded plant for every two or three seedless ones) so the bees can pollinate them. If fruit is not forming, grow some flowers nearby for the bees and try hand-pollinating in the morning.
seasoned: Watermelon is monoecious: each plant carries separate male and female flowers, so a standard seeded variety sets fruit on its own with no second variety needed. The flowers are insect-pollinated, mostly by bees, and watermelon is strongly pollinator-dependent, with each female flower needing many bee visits to set and size a full, well-filled melon. Poor pollination shows up as fruit that abort while small or grow lopsided and hollow-hearted. Seedless (triploid) watermelons are the exception that every grower must plan for: they produce no viable pollen of their own, so a seeded (diploid) pollinizer variety must be planted alongside, commonly one seeded plant for every two to three seedless plants, or a seeded row within about 10 feet, so bees can carry the pollen the seedless plants need. Plant flowers nearby, avoid spraying open blooms, and hand-pollinate in the morning if set is poor.

beginner: Watermelon is a warm-season vine that loves heat and sun and grows big, sweet, juicy fruit on long, trailing stems. Unlike summer squash that you pick again and again, you harvest a watermelon once, when it is fully ripe, and it will not ripen any more after you cut it, so picking at the right moment matters. The signs of a ripe melon are the little curly tendril next to the fruit drying up and turning brown, the pale spot where it sits on the ground turning creamy yellow, the skin going from shiny to dull, and a deep, dull thump when you tap it. The main things to know: give watermelon a long, hot summer, full sun, and warm soil, plenty of room to spread, and steady water while the fruit grows. Bees need to visit the flowers many times to set fruit. If you grow a seedless kind, you also have to plant a regular seeded variety nearby to pollinate it. Watch for cucumber beetles, aphids, spider mites, and several leaf and wilt diseases.
seasoned: Watermelon is a heat-loving, long-season trailing vine grown for its large, sweet, juicy fruit, a warm-season cousin of melon and squash in the cucumber family. It is harvested once at full ripeness rather than picked young and repeatedly, and it does not ripen further off the vine, so reading ripeness on the plant is the whole game: the curly tendril nearest the fruit dries and browns, the ground spot where the melon rests on the soil turns from white to a creamy yellow, the skin dulls from glossy to matte, and a ripe melon gives a deep, dull thump. The season's shape is set by three things: a long, hot runway (70 to 95 frost-free days with warm nights, so cool-summer northern and coastal areas are marginal), full sun and warm soil above 70°F at planting, and strong pollinator dependence, since each fruit needs many bee visits to set and size. Seedless (triploid) types add a wrinkle: they make no viable pollen of their own, so a seeded (diploid) pollinizer variety must be planted alongside to set fruit. The main pressures are cucumber beetles, aphids, and spider mites, plus the cucurbit diseases anthracnose, gummy stem blight, Fusarium wilt, and the mildews.

beginner: Pick a sunny spot with light, well-drained soil and mix in some compost before planting, but do not overdo rich, high-nitrogen material, or you get more vine than melon. seasoned: Prepare a deep, light, well-drained bed in full sun and work a few inches of compost into the soil before planting, easing off heavy nitrogen so the plant builds fruit rather than runaway vine. Most growers plant on low, wide hills or raised mounds, which warm faster, drain better, and give the trailing vines a starting point. Space generously: hills run roughly 4 to 8 feet apart with 6 to 8 feet between rows for full-size types (closer for icebox and bush kinds), because a full-size vine can run 8 to 12 feet and wants about 24 square feet to itself. Black plastic mulch is a real help in shorter or cooler-summer areas, warming the soil and speeding an early start. On heavy or wet ground, build the mounds up to improve drainage and head off wilt and fruit rot.
